essays.question: Many people think that public monuments should remain even if controversial. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Statues of generals, kings and traders stand in many city squares, and some of them are now seen as symbols of slavery, conquest or oppression, so many people think that public monuments should remain even if controversial. I agree to a large extent, since removing them can hide uncomfortable parts of the past, although some cases need special treatment.

To begin with, controversial monuments can be kept if their history is explained. Removing them can hide uncomfortable parts of the past, whereas plaques, museums and discussion help people to learn. A statue of a controversial figure that carries a plaque explaining his crimes, for example, teaches visitors more than an empty plinth. History is not always comfortable, and a society that erases every symbol that offends someone risks forgetting what happened and why. Monuments also show how attitudes have changed, since they reflect the values of the time in which they were built, and keeping them with context allows people to see how far society has moved. Public debate about them can itself be educational.

However, some monuments honour people responsible for great harm, and for communities that suffered, they can cause real pain. Decisions should therefore involve the affected community and clear criteria. In extreme cases, such as monuments that glorify genocide or mass violence, relocation to a museum may be justified, where they can be explained and studied instead of celebrated in a place of honour. Another option is to add new monuments that tell the stories of those who were ignored, so that the public landscape becomes more balanced. Destruction by crowds should be avoided, since decisions should be made lawfully and with debate.

In conclusion, public monuments should generally remain, even if controversial, provided that they are explained, and only in exceptional cases should they be moved, after open and fair discussion.

essays.question: Many people say that listening to music helps concentration. Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
Many people work or study with headphones on, and some say that listening to music helps concentration. I largely agree, although the benefit depends on the task and the type of music.

To begin with, music can help concentration on simple or repetitive tasks. Calm, familiar music blocks out noise and improves mood, which helps with routine work. A student who listens to quiet instrumental music while tidying notes, for example, may work faster and more happily, and many people report that music helps them to exercise, clean or draw. Music can also reduce stress and boredom, so people stay with a task for longer. In an open-plan office or a noisy home, a steady background of sound can mask distracting conversations and make it easier to focus. Studies suggest that people who enjoy their music perform better on certain tasks than those who work in silence.

However, music is not helpful for everything. Songs with lyrics compete with reading and writing, since the brain processes words in both, and the same student may find lyrics distracting during an essay. Unfamiliar, fast or loud music can draw attention away from demanding tasks such as learning new material or solving complex problems. People also differ: some find silence essential, while others cannot work without sound. The best approach is for each person to experiment, choosing instrumental or ambient music for demanding work and saving favourite songs for repetitive tasks or breaks. Volume should be kept low, since loud music can harm hearing as well as concentration.

In conclusion, I largely agree that listening to music helps concentration, particularly for simple tasks, but the effect depends on the task, the music and the individual.

essays.question: Is it better to focus government spending on arts or on sports development? Discuss and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Governments are regularly asked to fund new galleries, theatres, stadiums and sports programmes, and opinions are divided as to whether public money should go to the arts or to sports development. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of sports development argue that sport improves health and brings communities together. Regular exercise reduces obesity and heart disease, saves health costs and gives young people a positive way to spend their time. Sporting success also creates national pride and provides role models, and major events attract visitors and publicity. A new public swimming pool in a poorer district, for example, can give hundreds of children a place to exercise that their families could not otherwise afford. Sport teaches teamwork, discipline and resilience, and it often draws in young people who are not interested in more traditional cultural activities.

On the other hand, supporters of the arts point out that they develop creativity, cultural identity and mental wellbeing. Museums, theatres and music give people meaning and a sense of belonging, bring communities together and attract tourists. Arts education improves concentration and confidence, and cultural industries create many jobs. Without public support, many cultural activities would disappear, as they cannot survive on commercial income alone, whereas professional sport, with its television rights and sponsors, is often able to fund itself. Culture also records and passes on the stories of a society.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that a balanced budget is best, with sport funding concentrated on community and school facilities that improve public health, and arts funding directed to activities that the market would neglect.

essays.question: Some believe that national museums should display artifacts from other countries. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Museums in London, Paris and Berlin hold statues, jewellery and manuscripts from all over the world, and some believe that national museums should display artefacts from other countries. I agree to a large extent, since it widens understanding between cultures, although the way in which objects were acquired matters.

To begin with, displaying artefacts from other countries widens understanding and gives access to those who could never travel. National museums let visitors compare cultures and see objects that they would otherwise never be able to see, and a child in a small town can learn about ancient Egypt or China without leaving the country. Seeing the achievements of other peoples helps to challenge stereotypes and builds respect, and well-resourced museums can protect fragile objects with expert care. Such collections encourage scholars from different countries to study objects side by side and to share knowledge. Many museums also invite experts from the countries of origin to help with interpretation.

However, how objects were acquired matters. Many items were taken during colonial rule or without consent, so countries of origin ask for their return and see their display as a continuing injustice. A statue removed from a temple without permission, for example, may be returned or shared on loan after discussions between the museum and the country of origin. Items that were acquired legitimately, through purchase or gift, can remain on show, while those that were stolen or looted should be returned, or shared through long-term loans and digital access. Museums should also be open about the history of their collections and work in partnership with source communities. This approach allows people everywhere to enjoy shared heritage while respecting the rights of its owners.

In conclusion, national museums should display artefacts from other countries to a large extent, provided that they were acquired fairly and that disputed items are returned or shared.

essays.question: Discuss how cultural festivals support local economies.

versions.text:
Towns and cities across the world host film, food, music and heritage festivals, and many hope that they will benefit local economies. This essay will explain two key ways in which cultural festivals support local economies: through visitor spending and jobs, and through publicity and long-term investment.

First and foremost, cultural festivals bring money, jobs and publicity to the places that host them. Visitors spend on food, accommodation and souvenirs, stalls and performers earn income, and media coverage promotes the area. A potter who sells her work at a festival stall, for example, may earn in a weekend what she usually earns in a month. Festivals often take place outside the main holiday season, which fills hotels and restaurants that would otherwise be empty, and they create temporary jobs in security, catering, transport and cleaning. Local suppliers of food, drink and equipment also benefit, so that money circulates through the community instead of leaving it.

In addition, festivals can generate long-term benefits. A successful event can become part of a town's identity and attract visitors every year, and publicity may encourage investment in hotels, transport and facilities that continue to serve residents afterwards. Some visitors return in other seasons to explore more. However, the benefits are not guaranteed. Organising a festival costs money, much of the work is temporary, and large outside companies may receive most of the income if local businesses are not involved. Crowds and rubbish can also upset residents. Local businesses gain most when residents are involved in organising and supplying the event, and when the programme reflects the character of the place.

To sum up, cultural festivals support local economies by attracting visitors and spending and by building reputation, provided that they are well planned and involve local people. For these reasons, they deserve continued support.

analysis.type_vi: Opinion/discuss: lễ hội văn hoá hỗ trợ kinh tế địa phương như thế nào

plan.think: Mở bài nêu hiện tượng (nhiều thị trấn tổ chức liên hoan phim, ẩm thực, âm nhạc, di sản và hy vọng có lợi kinh tế) rồi hai cách: chi tiêu du khách và việc làm; quảng bá và đầu tư dài hạn.

Du khách chi cho thức ăn, chỗ ở, quà lưu niệm; gian hàng và nghệ sĩ có thu nhập; truyền thông quảng bá khu vực. Ví dụ thợ gốm bán ở gian hàng lễ hội kiếm trong cuối tuần bằng thu nhập thường cả tháng. Lễ hội ngoài mùa cao điểm lấp khách sạn, nhà hàng trống; việc làm tạm thời (an ninh, ăn uống, giao thông, dọn dẹp); nhà cung cấp địa phương hưởng lợi nên tiền luân chuyển trong cộng đồng.

plan.step: 3. Cách 2 — lợi ích dài hạn + giới hạn
plan.think: Sự kiện thành công thành bản sắc thị trấn, thu hút khách mỗi năm; quảng bá khuyến khích đầu tư khách sạn, giao thông, cơ sở tiếp tục phục vụ cư dân; khách quay lại. Giới hạn: không đảm bảo: tốn chi phí tổ chức, nhiều việc tạm thời; công ty lớn bên ngoài nhận phần lớn thu nếu doanh nghiệp địa phương không tham gia; đông đúc, rác phiền cư dân; lợi nhất khi cư dân tham gia tổ chức, cung ứng, chương trình phản ánh nơi.
Hỗ trợ kinh tế nếu lập kế hoạch tốt và có người địa phương tham gia; xứng đáng được tiếp tục ủng hộ.
